title: Commercial Insurance Prices Keep Falling Worldwide: Marsh Index Shows Property Down 12% While US Casualty Still Climbs 7%
summary: Marsh's latest detailed index shows global commercial rates down about 6% in Q2 2026, the eighth straight quarterly fall, with property down 12% and cyber down 4%, while US casualty rates rose 7%. Marsh's Q3 headline reportedly shows the decline slowing to about 5%.
description:
For businesses that buy insurance, the last two years have been unusually kind. Marsh, one of the world's largest insurance brokers, reports through its Global Insurance Market Index that commercial insurance rates around the world fell by about 6% on average in the second quarter of 2026, after a 5% decline in the first quarter. It was the eighth consecutive quarterly decrease. The index is built from the premium changes on the policies Marsh places for clients, so it measures what buyers actually paid at renewal compared with a year earlier, rather than what insurers say they are charging.

A note on the figures before going further. Marsh published its second-quarter release on July 23, 2026, and a more recent third-quarter release has since appeared. The trade publication The Insurer headlined its coverage of the third-quarter index as showing the global decrease "slowing to 5%", but that article is behind a subscription and Marsh's own third-quarter page could not be retrieved when this article was prepared. The regional and line-by-line numbers below therefore come from the fully published second-quarter release, and readers should check Marsh's index page for the newest quarter.

The decline is led by property insurance. Marsh reports that global property rates fell 12% in the second quarter, after falling 9% in both the first quarter of 2026 and the fourth quarter of 2025. By region, property rates dropped 19% in India, the Middle East and Africa, 15% in the Pacific, 14% in Latin America and the Caribbean, 13% in the United States, 11% in the United Kingdom, 9% in Europe, 8% in Canada and 5% in Asia. Casualty, which covers liability risks, moved in the opposite direction. Global casualty rates rose 2%, slower than the 3% rise in the first quarter. Outside the United States, every region saw casualty decreases, while US casualty rates rose 7%, down from 9% in the first quarter.

Financial and professional lines, the cover that protects directors, officers and professional advisers, fell 3% globally compared with a 5% fall in the previous quarter, with the United States the only region showing a modest increase. Cyber insurance fell 4% globally, the twelfth consecutive quarterly decline, with the steepest drop of 14% in India, the Middle East and Africa, 10% in Latin America and the Caribbean and 2% in the United States.

The regional composite figures show how uneven the softening is. India, the Middle East and Africa fell 16%, the Pacific 13%, Latin America and the Caribbean 9%, the United Kingdom 8%, Canada 7%, Europe 6% and Asia 5%. The United States was the most resilient market at a fall of just 2%, compared with a 1% fall in the first quarter. The reason is the weight of casualty business in American programmes. Liability costs in the US have been pushed up for years by large jury awards and the cost of litigation, often described as social inflation, so insurers there have kept raising casualty prices even as property rates drop.

Marsh attributes the broader trend to a combination of factors: strong insurer profitability, surplus capital, lower reinsurance costs and higher investment returns, all of which intensify competition for business. John Donnelly, president of global placement at Marsh Risk, said insurers are trying to stand out through broader coverage, expanded policy terms and lower deductibles. In other words, buyers are gaining not only lower prices but better terms.

The link to reinsurance matters. Primary insurers buy reinsurance to protect themselves against large losses, and when that cost falls, they can pass some of the saving to customers or use it to fund more competitive pricing. Separate coverage this week of the January 2027 reinsurance renewals suggests that source of softening has not run out: brokers and analysts are preparing for further reductions, as discussed in our coverage of the reinsurance market.

What does this mean for a business buyer? First, property buyers, particularly those outside the US, are in a strong negotiating position. Rates have been falling for several quarters, and insurers are competing on terms as well as price, so it is reasonable to ask for lower deductibles, broader perils and longer policy periods. Second, buyers of US liability insurance should not expect the same relief. Casualty rates are still rising there, although the pace has slowed from 9% to 7%, and insurers are cautious about the legal environment. Third, cyber buyers benefit from twelve straight quarters of falling prices, but cyber risk itself has not become smaller, so the sensible approach is to use the softer market to improve coverage and security controls rather than simply to cut spending.

For insurers, the picture is more mixed. Falling prices squeeze underwriting margins, but profitability is currently strong and catastrophe losses have been light in several recent quarters. Donnelly said current conditions are likely to persist absent a severe northern hemisphere storm season. That caveat is important. The soft market is a product of benign losses and abundant capital, and a major hurricane, earthquake or large systemic loss could change both quickly. Insurance cycles have turned before on exactly this kind of event.

Readers should also keep in mind what the index does and does not show. It reflects Marsh's client base, which skews toward larger and more complex buyers, and it measures changes in premium for comparable cover rather than the total amount a business spends, which can move with its own exposures and claims history. A company that grows, adds locations or has a bad claims year can see its bill rise even in a falling market. The headline figures are best read as a guide to the direction of the market, and every buyer's result will depend on its own risk profile.

The practical point is that the current market gives buyers leverage, but the leverage is not evenly spread across lines or countries and may not last. Businesses that start renewal preparation early, present their risk information clearly and compare options across insurers are most likely to turn a softening market into real savings and better protection.
source_name: Marsh (Global Insurance Market Index, Q2 2026 release of July 23, 2026) and The Insurer (Q3 2026 headline, October 15, 2026)
image_alt: Insurance documents and calculator representing commercial insurance pricing (illustrative)
key_points: Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index showed global commercial insurance rates falling about 6% in Q2 2026 after a 5% fall in Q1, the eighth consecutive quarterly decline.
Property rates fell 12% globally, casualty rates rose 2%, financial and professional lines fell 3% and cyber fell 4%, the twelfth straight quarterly decline for cyber.
The US was the outlier: composite rates fell only 2%, and US casualty rose 7% (down from 9% in Q1), while India, the Middle East and Africa fell 16% and the Pacific 13%.

Marsh attributes the softening to insurer profitability, surplus capital, lower reinsurance costs and higher investment returns, and says conditions are likely to persist absent a severe northern hemisphere storm season.
The Insurer's headline on Marsh's Q3 2026 index says the global decline slowed to about 5%; the full Q3 breakdown is behind a subscription, so the line-by-line figures here are from Q2.
why_it_matters: Commercial insurance is a cost for every business, so a long run of falling rates is good news for buyers: broader cover, lower deductibles and more negotiating power. But the pattern is uneven. US liability buyers are still paying more each quarter, and a bad storm season could reverse the trend quickly.

title: Reinsurers Brace for 10-15% Price Cuts at January 2027 Renewals as Hannover Re and Munich Re Defend Margins
summary: An analyst note signals property catastrophe rate cuts of 10-15% on January 1, 2027, while Munich Re's July renewals fell 5.5% and Hannover Re says it expects risk-adequate prices with terms broadly unchanged.
description:
The reinsurance market, which sells protection to insurance companies, is heading into its most important renewal date of the year with prices on the way down. On January 1 each year, a large share of the world's property catastrophe reinsurance contracts is renewed, and the results set the tone for pricing across the sector. Recent commentary from analysts and from two of Germany's largest reinsurers suggests that the January 1, 2027 renewals will bring further price cuts, though reinsurers insist that margins and contract terms remain healthy.

The sharpest signal comes from a note by the research firm Autonomous, reported by Reinsurance News on October 1, 2026. Autonomous says the messages coming out of the Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous, the annual gathering of reinsurers and brokers in September, appear to prepare the market for property catastrophe rate declines of 10-15% at the January renewals. If that proves correct, Autonomous argues, it would amount to a "full reversal of the hard market", at least on pricing. The hard market of 2022 and 2023 saw reinsurers raise prices sharply and tighten terms after several years of heavy catastrophe losses.

The article points to the supply of capital as the main reason. Aon estimates that total industry reinsurance capital stands at about $800 billion, which is 40% above the trough of 2022. Alternative capital, meaning money from investors rather than traditional reinsurers, has also grown. Aon puts sidecars, which are investor-backed vehicles that share in a reinsurer's risks, at around $23 billion at mid-year, up about 50% since the end of 2024. Autonomous estimates that vehicles focused on casualty business are much smaller, at little more than $2 billion. It also notes that the Marsh property catastrophe rate index signalled declines of about 16% through 2026, which suggests some natural slowing in the pace of decreases before the next fall.

What could stop the slide? Autonomous cites Gallagher Re's view that the market would need "well over $100 billion of excess losses" to restore stability. In plain terms, a normal run of catastrophes would not be enough; it would take an exceptional year to push prices back up. That makes the coming Atlantic hurricane season outcome and any large earthquake or other major event the key swing factors.

The two German reinsurers have spoken more cautiously about their own results. Munich Re reported that prices at its July 2026 renewals fell 5.5%, and that across the January, April and mid-year renewals this year the price decline averaged 3.1%. According to Artemis, which reported the figures on August 7, Munich Re's premium volume at the July renewals fell 9.1% to EUR 2.9 billion. The company explained that this reflects lower prices and its decision to decline business that did not meet its price or terms expectations. Property and casualty excess-of-loss business, where the reinsurer pays only once losses pass an agreed level, saw volume declines of more than 20%, with property excess-of-loss seeing the steepest price falls. Munich Re said its overall price level remains good despite the 5.5% decline, that terms and structures were largely unchanged, and that higher loss cost estimates driven by inflation and other trends were offset through pricing.

Looking ahead to January 2027, Munich Re said it expects the favourable price levels and improved terms to be "largely upheld despite the high level of competition". Its chief financial officer, Christoph Jurecka, said that over the medium term the company sees a compelling case for supply and demand in property and casualty reinsurance becoming more evenly balanced again. The company's first-half financial results show why it can afford that stance: net profit was EUR 3.925 billion compared with EUR 3.178 billion a year earlier, and the property and casualty reinsurance combined ratio was 68.9%, meaning claims and costs consumed well under 100% of premiums. Major losses in the second quarter were only EUR 191 million, far below the 18% of net insurance revenue that the company expects in a typical quarter. Munich Re maintained its full-year profit guidance of EUR 6.3 billion but cut its reinsurance revenue guidance to EUR 38 billion from EUR 40 billion, consistent with a market where it is writing less at lower prices.

Hannover Re, the other major German reinsurer, set out its view at the Monte Carlo press briefing in September. It expects generally risk-adequate rates across its property and casualty book, with terms and conditions likely to remain broadly unchanged, and says it will offer at least stable capacity provided that risk-adequate prices are available. It plans to grow where prices match risk, particularly in regions where insurance penetration and the economy are expanding, and sees strong demand for cyber, structured reinsurance and natural catastrophe covers. Regionally, it described Europe as broadly stable, North America as having sufficient capacity with property pricing still risk-adequate even though rate reductions are starting to appear, and Asia-Pacific as likely to see broadly stable or slightly softer rates in 2027. Competitive pressure is highest for natural catastrophe covers and loss-free business.

Autonomous also reports that brokers expect reinsurers to add "frequency" back into coverages, meaning that insurers may be asked to retain smaller losses less often, and that reinsurers have largely kept the improved terms won in the hard market while being willing to concede more on price. Investor interest in "ReShare" vehicles, a form of alternative capital, is described as a little counter-intuitive despite falling rates since new capital was largely absent when conditions were tighter in 2023 and 2024.

For the public, the effect of lower reinsurance costs is indirect and slow. Primary insurers set their own prices, taking into account claims, competition and regulation as well as reinsurance costs. Cheaper reinsurance gives them room to hold or reduce prices in catastrophe-exposed property lines, and the broker data on commercial insurance suggests that this is already happening. But it also raises a question of discipline. Insurers and reinsurers that cut prices aggressively in a quiet loss period can find themselves under-reserved or under-priced when a bad year arrives.

Two caveats apply to this reporting. The 10-15% figure is an analyst's reading of market messaging, not a published reinsurer forecast, and neither Munich Re nor Hannover Re gave a percentage for January 2027. Actual outcomes will depend on the loss experience of the final months of 2026 and on negotiations that continue into December.
source_name: Reinsurance News (Autonomous research, Oct 1, 2026), Artemis (Munich Re, Aug 7, 2026), Reinsurance News (Hannover Re, Sep 2026)
image_alt: Financial charts and documents representing reinsurance pricing (illustrative)
key_points: Analyst firm Autonomous says messages from the Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous point to property catastrophe rate declines of 10-15% at the January 1, 2027 renewals, which would be a full reversal of the hard market on pricing.
Aon estimates industry reinsurance capital at about $800 billion, up 40% from the 2022 trough, and sidecar capital at about $23 billion at mid-year, up about 50% since the end of 2024.
Munich Re said its July 2026 renewal prices fell 5.5% and premium volume fell 9.1% to EUR 2.9 billion, but it expects favourable prices and improved terms to be largely upheld in January 2027.
Hannover Re expects risk-adequate prices and broadly unchanged terms, will keep capacity at least stable, and notes rate reductions are starting to appear in North American property.
Gallagher Re is quoted as saying the market would need well over $100 billion of excess losses to restore stability, so a major catastrophe year is the main risk to the softening trend.
why_it_matters: Reinsurance is the insurance that insurers buy, and its price flows through to what households and businesses pay for property cover. Falling reinsurance rates can mean cheaper or broader property insurance later, but they also test whether insurers stay disciplined when competition grows.

title: Canada's June Prairie Storms Now Estimated at $923 Million in Insured Losses, With a Record 29,195 Hail Claims in Manitoba
summary: CatIQ's third estimate puts insured losses from the June 9-10 Prairie storms at $923 million, up from $728 million initially, driven latterly by commercial property; Manitoba Public Insurance received a record 29,195 hail claims.
description:
The cost of the severe storms that hit the Canadian Prairies in June has kept rising as insurers work through claims. According to the latest estimate from CatIQ, the firm that compiles Canada's industry catastrophe loss data, insured losses from the June 9-10, 2026 storms in Manitoba and Saskatchewan have reached $923 million. That is up from $850 million in CatIQ's 45-day estimate and from an initial post-event estimate of $728 million. Details of the third estimate were reported by Insurance Business Canada on September 10, 2026.

The pattern of the revisions is itself informative. CatIQ's earlier increase was mainly attributed to motor claims, which reflects the large number of vehicles damaged by hail. The most recent rise was driven by commercial property losses. This is typical of large hail events: vehicle claims arrive quickly because owners report damage immediately, while commercial buildings, with their roofs, cladding and contents, take longer to inspect, scope and settle. The $923 million figure is a total for insured losses only, and the source does not break it down by province or by auto and property.

CatIQ says the event now ranks third-highest by claims count in its catastrophe database. The storm system produced tornadoes, hail up to 10 centimetres in diameter, damaging winds and record rainfall. Provincial public insurers, which sell auto cover in both provinces, give a sense of the scale. Saskatchewan Government Insurance (SGI) expects more than $100 million in damage from the June 9 hailstorm in Regina, with about 13,000 claims. In Manitoba, Manitoba Public Insurance (MPI) received 29,195 hail-related claims from the same storm system, beating its previous record for a single event of about 24,000, set in 1996.

An earlier report from Reinsurance News on August 11, citing CatIQ at the time of its 45-day estimate, described insured losses above $840 million and said the storms affected tens of thousands of residents and businesses. It also noted that five of Canada's 11 catastrophic weather events so far in 2026 had affected the two provinces, including a dust storm that caused $40 million in insured losses. The August report gives "above $840 million" while the later article gives $850 million for the 45-day estimate; this article uses the later, more specific figure.

The longer trend is what concerns the industry. The Insurance Bureau of Canada (IBC) says that since 2021 Manitoba and Saskatchewan have experienced 30 catastrophic weather events with more than $2.5 billion in insured losses. That works out to nearly $1,000 per person over five years, a 140% increase compared with the previous five-year period. In 2025, wildfires caused about $430 million in insured losses in the two provinces, while flash flooding, hail and strong winds caused about $330 million. Aaron Sutherland of IBC said the trend "demands action". The bureau is urging governments to reduce exposure to extreme weather and has proposed incentives for retrofitting properties, stricter building codes, limits on development in high-risk flood and wildfire zones, and greater municipal investment in flood infrastructure.

CatIQ chief executive Laura Twidle said that 2026 "seems destined to be remembered for its storm-related flash flooding". That comment suggests that the Prairie losses are part of a wider season of intense rainfall events, not a single outlier, although the sources used for this article do not give national totals for the year to date.

Why do estimates keep rising after the storm? Insured loss estimates are built in stages. The initial figure is based on early reports and modelling. As adjusters inspect properties, claims are opened, and repair costs, supply shortages and building-code upgrade requirements become clearer, the total grows. The 45-day and later estimates draw on actual claims data from insurers. CatIQ will publish a fourth estimate on December 10, 2026, with more detailed loss data at the level of forward sortation areas, which are the first three characters of a postal code. That level of detail helps insurers and researchers see which neighbourhoods were hit hardest.

For homeowners and drivers, several practical points follow. Hail damage to vehicles is generally covered under the comprehensive section of an auto policy, while damage to a house is covered by home insurance, but deductibles and, in some cases, separate hail or wind deductibles apply. In provinces with public auto insurance, such as Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the public insurer handles auto claims, which is why MPI and SGI report the vehicle counts. Home and commercial property cover is sold by private insurers. Residents who have not yet filed a claim should check the time limits in their policies and keep photographs and repair estimates.

For the insurance market, the repeated losses raise questions about pricing and risk. Prairie hail has historically been a feature of the region, but the cost per event is climbing because more expensive homes, vehicles and buildings now sit in storm paths, and because repair costs have risen. The IBC's five-year comparison puts a number on this: a 140% rise in per-person insured loss. Premium increases and higher deductibles are common responses, and the bureau's proposed building-code and land-use measures aim to reduce the damage that occurs in the first place.

The $923 million estimate is likely to move again, and December's update will show whether claims from commercial property continue to grow or the total settles.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada (CatIQ third estimate, Sep 10, 2026) and Reinsurance News (CatIQ, Aug 11, 2026)
image_alt: Storm clouds over prairie farmland representing severe weather losses (illustrative)
key_points: CatIQ's third estimate puts insured losses from the June 9-10, 2026 Prairie storms at $923 million, up from $850 million at the 45-day mark and $728 million in the initial estimate.
The latest increase was driven mainly by commercial property losses, while the previous revision was mostly attributed to motor claims; the event ranks third by claims count in CatIQ's database.

Manitoba Public Insurance received 29,195 hail claims from the system, beating its single-event record of about 24,000 set in 1996; Saskatchewan's SGI expects over $100 million in damage and roughly 13,000 claims from the June 9 Regina hailstorm.

Since 2021, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have had 30 catastrophic weather events costing over $2.5 billion in insured losses, nearly $1,000 per person and a 140% rise on the previous five years, according to the Insurance Bureau of Canada.
A fourth CatIQ estimate with forward sortation area-level data is due December 10, 2026.
why_it_matters: Hail and flood damage is increasingly costly for Canadian households, and insured loss estimates tend to rise for months after a storm as claims are settled. The figures show why home and auto premiums in prairie provinces are under pressure and why the insurance industry is pressing for retrofit incentives and stricter building rules.

title: Sumitomo Life Sets Symetra Loose on a US Deal Hunt With Up to ¥1 Trillion to Invest as Japan's Insurers Keep Buying American
summary: Sumitomo Life has set aside up to ¥1 trillion (about $6.3 billion) for investments through March 2029 and will have Symetra lead the search for US deals, as Japanese life insurers such as Meiji Yasuda, Nippon Life and Daiichi continue to expand in America.
description:
Sumitomo Life, one of Japan's biggest life insurers, is preparing to spend heavily on overseas growth, and it wants its American subsidiary Symetra to find the deals. According to a report by Stephen Owens in Insurance Business on October 16, 2026, the Osaka-based group has set aside up to ¥1 trillion, about $6.3 billion, for investment under a business plan that runs through March 2029. President Yukinori Takada told Bloomberg News that the United States and Southeast Asia are the target regions, and Singapore's Income Insurance was named as a possible Asian target.

Symetra, which is headquartered in Bellevue, Washington, will lead the search in the US for businesses that complement what it already does. Takada said Sumitomo Life will not pursue overseas growth at any price. Insurance Business describes the aim as acquisitions that "fit alongside, not on top of" existing operations, which suggests a preference for adding capabilities or distribution rather than duplicating them.

Symetra's recent activity offers a clue to the kind of deals it may seek. In October 2025 it closed a reinsurance transaction to take over the life and disability book of Dearborn Group from Health Care Service Corporation (HCSC), together with a multiyear agreement to sell group products to HCSC's healthcare customers. The deal lifted Symetra's life and disability business to about $1.1 billion in annualized premium and added 2.5 million covered lives. Migration of Dearborn policies onto Symetra contracts is still under way. A deal built around reinsurance and a distribution agreement, rather than a full company purchase, is a template that may be repeated.

Sumitomo Life has owned Symetra since February 2016, when it completed a takeover worth roughly $3.8 billion that took the company private from the New York Stock Exchange. Symetra kept its brand, management and Seattle-area headquarters. With consolidated total assets of about ¥51.6 trillion, or $322.6 billion, at the end of March, Sumitomo Life ranks fifth among Japan's life insurers, behind Nippon Life, Daiichi, Meiji Yasuda and Japan Post Insurance.

The strategy fits a broader pattern. Japanese life insurers have been among the most active foreign buyers of American insurance businesses. Meiji Yasuda bought StanCorp Financial, the parent of The Standard, in 2016 and completed a $2.3 billion purchase of Legal & General America in February 2026, adding Banner Life and a share of the pension risk transfer business. Nippon Life paid $3.8 billion for a 20% stake in Corebridge Financial in 2024, later completed its acquisition of Resolution Life and folded Resolution's US, UK and Bermuda operations into a new division, and nominates a director to Corebridge's board. Dai-ichi Life, now called Daiichi Life Group, has owned Protective Life of Birmingham, Alabama, since 2015.

Why are Japanese insurers looking abroad? The article does not spell out the motives, but they are widely understood. Japan's population is shrinking and ageing, which limits growth in domestic life insurance. The United States is the world's largest life and annuity market, with strong demand for retirement products and a large pool of assets, and has a long record of open acquisitions by foreign insurers. Buying an established American business gives a Japanese insurer diversification and access to a different growth cycle. These points are context rather than statements from the Insurance Business report.

Competition for deals is stiff. The report notes that Allianz beat Sumitomo Life to HSBC's Singapore life business earlier in 2026. Asia and the US are both busy markets for insurance acquisitions, with private equity, other insurers and sovereign investors all competing. PwC's recent review of US insurance mergers found that megadeals drove most of the deal value in the six months to May 2026 and that demand for life and annuity platforms remains strong although sponsors are more selective.

What would a Symetra-led acquisition look like in practice? It could be a block of life or disability policies, a group benefits business, a distribution partner or a specialist administrator. The source does not name any target or give a timetable, and Takada's comments were general. No deal has been announced. The ¥1 trillion figure is an upper limit for investment across the plan's regions and purposes, not a budget dedicated to a single purchase.

For American customers, such deals normally do not change their policy terms, since existing contracts transfer with the business and remain regulated by state insurance departments. For the industry, more Japanese ownership brings long-term capital that is comfortable holding policies for decades, but it also ties American insurers more closely to Japanese corporate decisions and to exchange-rate and interest-rate movements in Japan.

For investors and policymakers, the key questions will be how disciplined Sumitomo Life is on price, as it says, and how it balances the US against Southeast Asia, where it has already lost one bidding contest. Symetra's integration of the Dearborn book will also be an early test of its ability to digest larger transactions.
image_alt: Tokyo skyline representing Japanese life insurers expanding abroad (illustrative)
key_points: Sumitomo Life has set aside up to ¥1 trillion (about $6.3 billion) for investment under a business plan running to March 2029, targeting the US and Southeast Asia, according to its president Yukinori Takada.
Symetra, which Sumitomo Life has owned since February 2016 after a takeover worth roughly $3.8 billion, will lead the US search for businesses that complement its existing lines.

Last October Symetra took over Dearborn Group's life and disability book from Health Care Service Corporation, lifting its life and disability business to about $1.1 billion of annualized premium and adding 2.5 million covered lives.

Meiji Yasuda completed a $2.3 billion purchase of Legal & General America in February 2026; Nippon Life paid $3.8 billion for a 20% stake in Corebridge in 2024; Dai-ichi has owned Protective Life since 2015.
Allianz beat Sumitomo Life to HSBC's Singapore life business earlier in 2026, and Singapore's Income Insurance is named as a possible Asian target.
why_it_matters: Japan's ageing population and low domestic growth are pushing its large life insurers to buy growth abroad, especially in the United States. That affects American annuity and life insurance markets, which increasingly have Japanese owners, and it shapes where billions of dollars of savings are invested.

title: IRDAI's 137th Authority Meeting Approves Seven Insurance Regulations to Implement the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, Including a New Policyholder Protection Fund
summary: At its 137th meeting on July 28, 2026, chaired by Ajay Seth, IRDAI approved seven regulations aligning the rulebook with the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025, including the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund Regulations and stricter intermediary rules aimed at curbing mis-selling.
description:
India's insurance regulator has taken a batch of decisions that will shape how insurers, brokers and agents operate under the country's recently amended insurance laws. According to a summary of the minutes published by TaxGuru, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) held its 137th Authority meeting on July 28, 2026, at 3 pm at its headquarters. Chairman Ajay Seth chaired the meeting, and part-time member Dr. Debasish Prusty joined virtually. The Authority approved seven sets of regulations after considering stakeholder comments, consultations with the Insurance Advisory Committee on July 21, 2026, and comments from the Department of Financial Services on July 27, 2026.

Most of the regulations bring IRDAI's framework into line with the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendments to Insurance Laws) Act, 2025. The stated aims, according to the minutes summary, include ease of doing business, simpler processes, lower compliance costs and stronger oversight. Each regulation had been issued as an exposure draft in June 2026 for public comment, so the approvals follow a consultation period of about five to six weeks.

The first approval is the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund Regulations, 2026, issued in draft on June 23. They set the governance, funding and use of the fund created under the 2025 Act. The fund draws on grants, donations and penalties, and its purposes include protecting policyholders, educating them and raising awareness, and promoting financial inclusion. The summary does not describe how money will be allocated or how much the fund is expected to hold.

The second is the Manner and Procedure for Imposition of Penalties Regulations, 2026, issued in draft on June 19. These set out how IRDAI imposes penalties for defaults or contraventions under the Insurance Act, 1938, the IRDA Act, 1999, and related rules and regulations. Clear procedure matters because penalties that are not applied through a transparent process can be challenged on appeal. The summary does not state penalty amounts.

Third, the Authority approved the Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026, which strengthen the prudential framework and actuarial oversight with an emphasis on operational clarity and rationalised processes. Fourth came the Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, issued in draft on June 15. These align the rules with the revised provisions of the Insurance Act and are intended to facilitate capital infusion.

Fifth, the Third Party Administrators (Health Services) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 align the framework for TPAs, the firms that process health insurance claims on behalf of insurers, with the 2025 Act.

The sixth item is probably the most significant for ordinary customers: the Insurance Intermediaries (Amendment) Regulations, 2026. They amend five existing regulations covering corporate agents (2015), insurance brokers (2018), insurance marketing firms (2015), web aggregators (2017) and common public service centres (2019). The stated goals are to make intermediaries accountable for their sales staff, to tighten oversight of sales practices in order to curb mis-selling and to improve transparency. Mis-selling, such as pushing an unsuitable product or misrepresenting a policy's benefits, is a recurring consumer complaint in Indian insurance, and making intermediary firms answerable for the conduct of individual salespeople gives them an incentive to train and supervise them.

The seventh is the Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (Amendment) Regulations, 2026. These revise the licensing framework for surveyors and loss assessors, the professionals who assess damage in general insurance claims, to create a more transparent registration system, add offsite annual compliance monitoring and improve digital services.

The meeting also dealt with the regulator's own accounts. The summary says the Comptroller and Auditor General issued a preliminary draft separate audit report on May 8, 2025. IRDAI responded on May 27, 2026, and the final report was issued on July 21, 2026. The Authority adopted IRDAI's 2024-25 Annual Statement of Accounts and authorised the chairperson to handle the CAG's queries, forward the certified accounts and audit report to the central government, and publish the CAG's observations, IRDAI's response and the annual accounts.

There are limits to what can be concluded. The source summarises the minutes; it does not reproduce the detailed provisions, thresholds or penalty amounts, and it does not say when the regulations take effect or when they will be notified in the Gazette. Until the regulations are notified, insurers and intermediaries cannot treat them as in force, and readers should consult IRDAI's website for the final text.

What should consumers and businesses watch for? Policyholders should look for more explicit accountability from intermediaries, including clearer disclosures at the point of sale. Insurers should expect changes in how penalties are decided and in capital-raising rules. Brokers, agents and web aggregators will need to update their compliance and training processes. And the new protection fund will matter if it is funded and used as described, because it could support education campaigns and redress mechanisms.

The wider context is the government's goal of broader insurance coverage, which the 2025 Act supports with changes to the law. Regulations are where such principles become operational rules, so the content of the notified texts, rather than the headlines about their approval, will determine the impact on customers.
image_alt: Legal documents and a gavel representing insurance regulation in India (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI's Authority met for the 137th time on July 28, 2026 under chairman Ajay Seth and approved seven sets of regulations, mostly to align the framework with the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendments to Insurance Laws) Act, 2025.

The Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund Regulations, 2026 set governance, funding and use rules for a fund drawing on grants, donations and penalties to protect and educate policyholders and promote financial inclusion.

New penalty-procedure regulations set out how IRDAI imposes penalties under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, and amended rules cover actuarial functions, insurer registration and capital structure, and third party administrators.
The Insurance Intermediaries (Amendment) Regulations amend five sets of rules, making intermediaries accountable for their sales staff and tightening oversight of sales practices to curb mis-selling.
The source does not give detailed provisions, penalty amounts or effective dates, so these must be checked in the notified regulations.
why_it_matters: Insurance buyers in India are often exposed to mis-selling and slow claims. These regulations determine how insurers are supervised, how penalties are applied and how intermediaries are held accountable, and they build the legal machinery behind a national fund meant to protect policyholders.

title: UK Motor Insurance Prices Rise for the First Time in Three Years as Insurers Pay Out a Record £3.2 Billion in a Quarter
summary: Defaqto data show competitive UK motor premiums 2.7% higher in September than a year earlier, the first annual rise since 2023, while the ABI reports record quarterly claims payouts of £3.2 billion and an average premium of £566 in Q2 2026.
description:
After two years of falling prices, UK car insurance is getting more expensive again. The latest Defaqto data, reported by Insurance Edge on October 15, 2026, show that competitive quoted premiums at the end of September were 2.7% higher than in September 2025. That is the first annual increase since 2023, following price cuts in 2024 and 2025. Defaqto's Market Pricing Motor Insurance Price Index is based on quoted prices rather than prices actually paid, and the article does not give an average premium in pounds, so the data are best read as a measure of direction.

The increase has been gradual. Quarterly growth slowed to 0.5% in the third quarter, down from 2.1% in the second quarter. The average of the top five quoted premiums rose 0.4% in July and 0.2% in August, then fell 0.1% in September. The third quarter was the third consecutive quarter of growth, and prices rose 2.6% over the six months to the end of September. Perspective matters: premiums remain 12.8% below their level two years earlier, although they are 11.9% above where they stood at the start of 2020. Drivers have not yet seen a return to the peak, but the direction has changed.

The average hides large differences. Among providers, third-quarter price movements ranged from a fall of 3.5% to a rise of 9.6%, so some insurers are still cutting while others are pushing up. By age, older drivers saw the largest annual increases, while drivers under 26 and those aged 26 to 30 were still paying less than a year earlier. Movements by annual mileage band were more even, though drivers with lower mileage saw bigger increases. The regional spread was wide, from a fall of 1% in London to a rise of 16.3% in Northern Ireland. A driver's experience at renewal will therefore depend heavily on where they live, how old they are and which insurer they use.

Claims data from the Association of British Insurers (ABI) help explain why the price decline has ended. On July 30, 2026, the ABI reported, as covered by Insurance Times, that motor insurers paid out a record £3.2 billion in claims in the second quarter of 2026. That was 5% higher than in the first quarter and 7% above the second quarter of 2025. The average payout rose 4% to £4,900 compared with the first quarter. The ABI partly attributes higher costs to pricier repairs, as modern vehicles depend more on cameras, sensors and driver assistance systems. Even windscreens are affected: windscreen repair bills rose 7% to an average of £283.

The ABI also reported that the average premium climbed £6 to £566 in the second quarter, a 1% quarterly rise. After adjusting for inflation, it was £14 lower than in the second quarter of 2025, so in real terms premiums were still cheaper than a year earlier at that point. This helps to reconcile the two data sets. The ABI figure measures the average premium customers actually paid, and it is a lagging measure, while Defaqto measures quoted prices at a point in time. Quoted prices have begun to rise, and the ABI average may follow.

Chris Bose, the ABI's director of general insurance and international policy, said motor insurers are working hard to keep premiums competitive and affordable. He called on the government to help address claims inflation by building skills in the repair sector and improving the availability of parts, and he pointed to the Motor Insurance Taskforce as an opportunity to work with the government.

The dynamics here are straightforward. When premiums fall for a prolonged period while claims costs rise, insurers' margins narrow. Eventually, insurers raise prices to restore profit. The record quarterly payouts and the end of the price decline fit that pattern. The sources used here do not report insurers' profit margins or combined ratios, so the extent of the pressure cannot be measured from them.

There are also reasons the rise may stay modest. Competition is still strong, and the quarterly increase of 0.5% was much smaller than the 2.1% of the previous quarter. Several providers are still cutting, which shows that competition for customers remains alive.

What can drivers do? Because the range of price movements between providers is so wide, comparing quotes at every renewal is likely to produce more savings than usual. Using price comparison sites, checking cover as well as price, and being accurate about mileage and usage can all help. Drivers with lower annual mileage, who the data show have been facing bigger increases, may want to check whether a lower-mileage policy or a telematics product suits them. Older drivers, who have seen the largest rises, should ask about discounts and compare across insurers rather than automatically renewing. Residents of Northern Ireland, where quotes were up 16.3% on the year, are especially likely to benefit from shopping around.

The long-term fix, the ABI argues, lies in the cost of claims: repair skills, parts supply and vehicle technology. Until these costs ease, premiums are more likely to rise than fall, and the question for 2027 is whether competition between insurers can keep increases small.
source_name: Insurance Edge (Defaqto Q3 2026 data, Oct 15, 2026) and Insurance Times (ABI Q2 2026 motor figures, July 30, 2026)
